newsitem.title: USA: Court hears arguments in landmark phone case.
newsitem.headline: Court hears arguments in landmark phone case.

text.p: A U.S. court heard arguments on Thursday on whether or not to allow a landmark rule to take effect that would pry open the nation's local telephone monopolies, with judges raising questions over key parts of the measure.

The Eighth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard lawyers' arguments on whether or not to uphold a temporary freeze of new Federal Communications Commission rules designed to open the $100 billion local telephone market to long-distance carriers, cable television operators and others.
Former U.S. Attorney General William Barr, now chief counsel of GTE Corp, said it was difficult to guess what the justices would decide, but he was "optimistic."

"I was very pleased with the way (our) argument went this morning," he told reporters. Brad Ramsay, assistant general counsel for the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, also was optimistic.
"It's always difficult based upon what judge says, but by the questions asked, you could tell that the judges favored the states' views on pricing," Ramsay told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Mark Rosenblum, vice president of law and public policy for AT&T declined comment when asked for his reaction. A spokesman for AT&T said there was "no indication" as to what the judges might decide.

Barr argued the FCC had no authority to impose price rules on state regulators who oversee negotiations between the Baby Bells and other local telephone companies and long- distance carriers and others trying to hook up to the local network.
Barr also argued the agency's pricing rules were "arbitary" and did not accord with the standards of the telecommunications law enacted in February.
Diane Munns, general counsel of the Iowa Utilities Board, agreed with Barr and also argued that the FCC rules left little leeway for state regulators.
Chris Wright, representing the FCC, said the FCC had exclusive rights to make rules in regards to the the new law.
"The FCC makes the rules and the states are left with the very difficult task of applying those rules," Wright said.

However, Judge Pasco Bowman, who presided over the appeal, questioned Wright's argument. "There's no doubt that the FCC has rule-making authority, but what kind of rules? That's the issue we're faced with here," Bowman said at one point.
Bowman also questioned arguments made by David Carpenter, who represented AT&T and other long-distance carriers.
Carpenter argued he local phone companies would suffer no immediate financial harm if the court lifted the stay order.
An appeals court in St. Louis issued the order last week, freezing the rules that would have taken effect this week.
They require the Baby Bells and other local carriers to lease local lines in bulk to competitors at discounts of 17 to 25 percent below retail prices.
The agency also ordered local carriers to "unbundle" their local networks into seven segments that new rivals can lease. These include call-switching devices and operator and directory assistance.

These "unbundled elements" are to be priced at competitive levels based on the cost of new and more-efficient facilities. The Bells have argued that prices should instead reflect the original cost of the technology, which is more expensive.
